One shall see from  Lemma~\ref{lem-DF} below that,  under the assumption of Theorem~\ref{thm-fourier},   the following  implication holds: 
\[
\mathbb{E} [ W^{(2)}\log W^{(2)}] \le \log b \Longrightarrow \mathbb{E}[W^2]<b. 
\]
Moreover, if  the random weight $W$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[W^2]<b$, then (see \S \ref{S-second moment} in the Appendix) 
	\begin{align}\label{2-m-intuition}
	\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(k)|^2] \asymp k^{-(1-\frac{\log \mathbb{E}[W^2]}{\log b})} \quad \text{as $\mathbb{N}\ni k\to\infty$}.
	\end{align}
Therefore,  here the asymptotic in the average sense \eqref{2-m-intuition}  gives a correct prediction of the almost sure asymptotics of $|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(k)|$ and thus the Fourier dimension of $\mu_\infty$: 
\[
\dim_F(\mu_\infty)= D_F = 1-\frac{\log \mathbb{E}[W^2]}{\log b}. 
\]

Let mu be a finite positive Borel measure supported on [delta, 1 - delta] for some 0< delta<1/2 and let Psi(t) be a positive function on (0, infty) which is decreasing on [t_0, infty) for some t_0>0 and such that Psi (t/2)=O(Psi(t)) as ttoinfty. Then widehatmu(n)=O(Psi(|n|)) \,\,as\,\, n rightarrow infty Longrightarrow widehatmu(zeta)=O(Psi(|zeta|)) \,\,as\,\, zeta rightarrow infty. Clearly, the support assumption of Kahane can be replaced by the assumption that mu is supported on a sub-interval of length strictly less than 1. Lemma is obtained as follows: we may assume that mu is a probability measure and X stackreld=P_X = mu. Then Z = X/2 is supported on [0, 1/2] and widehatmu(zeta) = widehatP_X(zeta)= E[exp(-i 2 pi X zeta) ]= E[exp(-i 2 pi Z 2 zeta) ] = widehatP_Z(2zeta). Since P_Z is supported on the interval [0,1/2] of length strictly less than 1, we may apply Kahane's result and obtain \[ widehatmu(n/2) = widehatP_Z(n) = O(n^-D/2) \,\,as\,\, n rightarrow infty Longrightarrow widehatmu(zeta/2) = widehatP_Z(zeta) = O(zeta^-D/2) \,\,as\,\, zeta rightarrow infty. \] Lemma~ is proved in a slightly different way. Indeed, we shall prove that \[ widehatmu(n) = O(n^-D/2) \,\,as\,\, n rightarrow infty Longrightarrow widehatmu(zeta) = O(|zeta|^-D/2 log |zeta|) \,\,as\,\, zeta rightarrow infty. \] More precisely, in Proposition~, we prove that if |widehatmu(n)| = O(n^-kappa) with kappa in (0, 1], then \[ |widehatmu_0(n)| = O(n^-kappa log n) \, and \, |widehatmu_1(n)| = O(n^-kappa log n), \] where mu_0 = mu|_[0,1/2) and mu_1= mu|_[1/2, 1] are the restrictions of mu on two sub-intervals of length 1/2. We can then apply Kahane's result to mu_0 and mu_1 respectively and obtain \[ |mu(zeta)| le |mu_0(zeta)| + |mu_1(zeta)| = O big( |zeta|^-kappa log (|zeta|)big) \, as \, zeta to infty. \]

\label{rem-ka}
  Kahane \cite[Chapter 17, Lemma 1]{Kahane-book} actually proved  more. Here we present a version that is suitable for our purpose. Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure supported on $[\delta, 1 - \delta]$ for some $0< \delta<1/2$ and let  $\Psi(t)$ be  a positive function on $(0, \infty)$ which is decreasing on $[t_0, \infty)$ for some $t_0>0$ and  such that $\Psi (t/2)=O(\Psi(t))$ as $t\to\infty$. Then 
 \begin{align}\label{Kah-rel}
  \widehat{\mu}(n)=O(\Psi(|n|))  \text{\,\,as\,\,} n \rightarrow \infty  \Longrightarrow \widehat{\mu}(\zeta)=O(\Psi(|\zeta|))   \text{\,\,as\,\,} \zeta \rightarrow \infty. 
  \end{align}
 Clearly, the support assumption of Kahane can be replaced by the assumption that $\mu$ is supported on a sub-interval of length strictly less than $1$.  Lemma \ref{lem-trans-coef-bis}  is obtained as follows: we may assume that $\mu$ is a probability measure and $X \stackrel{d}{=}\mathbb{P}_X = \mu$.  Then  $Z = X/2$ is supported on $[0, 1/2]$  and $\widehat{\mu}(\zeta)  = \widehat{\mathbb{P}_X}(\zeta)= \mathbb{E}[\exp(-i 2 \pi X \zeta) ]= \mathbb{E}[\exp(-i 2 \pi Z 2 \zeta) ] = \widehat{\mathbb{P}_Z}(2\zeta)$.  Since $\mathbb{P}_Z$ is supported on the interval $[0,1/2]$ of length strictly less than $1$, we may apply Kahane's result \eqref{Kah-rel} and obtain 
 \[
 \widehat{\mu}(n/2) = \widehat{\mathbb{P}_Z}(n) = O(n^{-D/2})  \text{\,\,as\,\,} n \rightarrow \infty   \Longrightarrow  \widehat{\mu}(\zeta/2) = \widehat{\mathbb{P}_Z}(\zeta) = O(\zeta^{-D/2})  \text{\,\,as\,\,} \zeta \rightarrow \infty. 
 \]
Lemma~\ref{lem-trans-coef} is  proved in a slightly different way.  Indeed, we shall prove that 
\[
 \widehat{\mu}(n) = O(n^{-D/2})  \text{\,\,as\,\,} n \rightarrow \infty   \Longrightarrow  \widehat{\mu}(\zeta) = O(|\zeta|^{-D/2} \log |\zeta|)  \text{\,\,as\,\,} \zeta \rightarrow \infty. 
\]
More precisely,   in  Proposition~\ref{lem-Fdecay},  we prove that  if $|\widehat{\mu}(n)|  = O(n^{-\kappa})$ with $\kappa \in (0, 1]$, then 
\[
|\widehat{\mu}_0(n)|  = O(n^{-\kappa} \log n) \text{\, and \,}  |\widehat{\mu}_1(n)| = O(n^{-\kappa} \log n),
\]
where $\mu_0 = \mu|_{[0,1/2)}$ and $\mu_1= \mu|_{[1/2, 1]}$ are the restrictions of $\mu$ on two sub-intervals of length $1/2$. We can then apply Kahane's result  \eqref{Kah-rel}  to $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$ respectively and obtain 
\[
|\mu(\zeta)| \le    |\mu_0(\zeta)|  + |\mu_1(\zeta)|   = O  \big( |\zeta|^{-\kappa} \log (|\zeta|)\big) \text{\, as \,} \zeta \to \infty.
\]

\label{prop-clt}
Assume that $\mathbb{E}[W\log W]<\log b$ and $\mathbb{E}[W^t]<\infty$ for all $t>0$.  We have the following convergences in distribution  under $\mathbb{P}^* = \mathbb{P}(\cdot | \mu_\infty\ne 0)$:
\begin{itemize}
\item Squared sub-critical regime: if $\mathbb{E}[ W^{(2)} \log W^{(2)}] < \log b$ and $b\ge 3$, then 
\[
b^{\frac{nD_F}{2}} \cdot  \widehat{\mu}_\infty(b^n)  \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\quad d \quad }      \sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^2] \cdot  \mathscr{M}_\infty(W^{(2)})} \cdot \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{C}}(0,1),
\]
where $\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{C}}(0,1)$ is  independent of $\mathscr{M}_\infty(W^{(2)})$ and $\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^2]\in (0,\infty) $ is given in \eqref{eqn-mu-s-square-s=1}. 
\item  Squared critical regime:  if $\mathbb{E}[ W^{(2)} \log W^{(2)}]  = \log b$ and $b \ge 3$, then 
\[
n^{\frac{1}{4}} \cdot b^{\frac{nD_F}{2}} \cdot  \widehat{\mu}_\infty(b^n)  \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\quad d \quad }      \sqrt{ \mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^2] \cdot  \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi \sigma^2}}  \mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})} \cdot \mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{C}}(0,1),
\]
where $\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})$ is the a.s. limit of the derivative martingale of BRW,  coming from the Seneta-Heyde norming limit of the $\mathscr{M}_n(W^{(2)})$  proved in \cite{Aideon-Shi} as follows: 
\[
 \sqrt{n} \cdot  \mathscr{M}_n(W^{(2)}) \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\text{in probability}} \mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)}) \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi \sigma^2}} 
\]
   with $\sigma^2\in(0,\infty)$ given in \eqref{def-BRW-var} and  $\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{C}}(0,1)$  independent of $\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})$.
   \item Squared super-critical regime:  if $\mathbb{E}[ W^{(2)} \log W^{(2)}] > \log b$ and $\log W$ is non-lattice, then there exists  a unique constant $\beta\in (1/2,1)$ depending only on $W$ (see \eqref{def-beta}), such that  
 \begin{align*}
b^{\frac{n D_F}{2}}n^{\frac{3}{2}\beta} \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^{n}\right)\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{d}  \mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})^\beta \sum_{x \in \mathcal{Z}_\infty} e^{-\beta x}\widehat{\mu}^{(x)}_\infty(1),
 \end{align*}
 where $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$ is a  decorated Poisson point process  (see  \eqref{eqn-z-infinity-s}), given $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$, $\{\widehat{\mu}^{(x)}_\infty(1)\}_{x\in \mathcal{Z}_\infty}$ are i.i.d. copies of $\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)$,  and $\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})$ is independent of $(\mathcal{Z}_\infty, \{\widehat{\mu}^{(x)}_\infty(1)\}_{x\in \mathcal{Z}_\infty})$.  Moreover, the real part of $ \sum_{x \in \mathcal{Z}_\infty} e^{-\beta x}\widehat{\mu}^{(x)}_\infty(1)$ has a $\frac{1}{\beta}$-stable law. 
\end{itemize}

\mathbb{E}[W^p]<b^{p-1} \Longleftrightarrow \|W\|_{L^{p-1}(W \mathbb{P})} = \Big( \int  W^{p-1} \cdot Wd\mathbb{P}\Big)^{\frac{1}{p-1}} <b.
\]

\]

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition \ref{prop-mart-type}
nodes.statement: Recall the definition of martingale type p of a Banach space. Consider the martingale (M_n^V)_nge 1 defined in . By the martingale type p assumption on X, there exists C>0 such that for any Nge 1, \[ E[\|M_N^V \|_X^p] le C sum_n=0^N E[\|dM_n^V \|_X^p], \] Now for each nge 1, since \mathringW(u): |u|=n\ are mutually independent centered random variables, with respect to the conditional expectation E_n-1[cdot] = E[cdot|F_n-1], we apply again the martingale type p inequality to the expression for dM_n^V and obtain E_n-1[ \|dM_n^V\|_X^p] & = E_n-1Big[ Big\| sum_|u|=n Big(prod_j=0^n-1 W(u|_j)Big) mathringW(u) cdot V(I_u) Big\|_X^p Big] \\ & le C sum_|u|=n E_n-1Big[ Big\| Big(prod_j=0^n-1 W(u|_j)Big) mathringW(u) cdot V(I_u) Big\|_X^pBig] \\ & = C E[|mathringW(u)|^p] cdot sum_|u|=n Big(prod_j=0^n-1 W(u|_j)^p Big) cdot \| V(I_u) \|_X^p. Hence, by E[|mathringW|^p] le 2^p E[W^p], we have \[ E[ \|dM_n^V\|_X^p] le C 2^p (E[W^p])^n cdot sum_|u|=n \| V(I_u) \|_X^p. \] By noting the equality \[ \|T_n^V\|_L^p(X)^p = b^n(p-1) sum_|u|=n \| V(I_u)\|_X^p, \] we complete the proof of the proposition.

Recall the definition \eqref{def-Mtype} of martingale type $p$ of a Banach space.   Consider the martingale $(M_n^\mathcal{V})_{n\ge 1}$  defined in   \eqref{def-mart}.
By the martingale type $p$ assumption on $\mathbb{X}$, there exists $C>0$ such that for any $N\ge 1$, 
\[
\mathbb{E}[\|M_N^\mathcal{V} \|_{\mathbb{X}}^p] \le C   \sum_{n=0}^N \mathbb{E}[\|dM_n^\mathcal{V} \|_{\mathbb{X}}^p],
\]
Now for each $n\ge 1$, since $\{\mathring{W}(u): |u|=n\}$ are mutually independent centered random variables, with respect to the conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}_{n-1}[\cdot] = \mathbb{E}[\cdot|\mathscr{F}_{n-1}]$,   we  apply again the martingale type $p$ inequality \eqref{def-ind-Mtype}  to the expression \eqref{def-dM} for $dM_n^\mathcal{V}$  and obtain 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}_{n-1}[ \|dM_n^\mathcal{V}\|_{\mathbb{X}}^p]  & =    \mathbb{E}_{n-1}\Big[   \Big\|  \sum_{|u|=n}  \Big(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} W(u|_j)\Big) \mathring{W}(u) \cdot \mathcal{V}(I_u)   \Big\|_{\mathbb{X}}^p \Big]  
\\
&  \le C    \sum_{|u|=n}    \mathbb{E}_{n-1}\Big[ \Big\| \Big(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} W(u|_j)\Big) \mathring{W}(u) \cdot \mathcal{V}(I_u)   \Big\|_{\mathbb{X}}^p\Big]
\\
& = C   \mathbb{E}[|\mathring{W}(u)|^p]    \cdot    \sum_{|u|=n}     \Big(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1} W(u|_j)^p \Big)  \cdot     \| \mathcal{V}(I_u)   \|_{\mathbb{X}}^p. 
\end{align*}
Hence, by $\mathbb{E}[|\mathring{W}|^p] \le 2^p  \mathbb{E}[W^p]$, we have 
\[
\mathbb{E}[ \|dM_n^\mathcal{V}\|_{\mathbb{X}}^p]  \le   C  2^p (\mathbb{E}[W^p])^{n}  \cdot    \sum_{|u|=n}       \| \mathcal{V}(I_u)   \|_{\mathbb{X}}^p.  
\]
By noting the equality
\[
\|T_n^\mathcal{V}\|_{L^p(\mathbb{X})}^p = b^{n(p-1)} \sum_{|u|=n}  \| \mathcal{V}(I_u)\|_{\mathbb{X}}^p, 
\]
we complete the proof of the proposition.

 \|T_n^\mathcal{V}\|_{L^p(\mathbb{X})}^p  \le       \Big(  \frac{b^{p-1}}{\mathbb{E}[W^p]}  \Big)^n    e^{-n \delta} \quad  \text{for large enough $n$}.

Clearly,  for any $u\in \mathcal{A}^*$ with $1\le |u|\le N$, 
\[
\mathbb{E}_{u^{-}}\Big[\big\|  D_u \big[ M_N^\mathcal{V}\big] \big \|_{\ell^q}^q\Big]  =   \mathbb{E}\big[ |\mathring{W}|^q \big] \cdot  \Big(  \prod_{j=0}^{|u|-1} W(u|_j)^q \Big)   \cdot  \|\mathcal{V}(I_u)\|_{\ell^q}^q .
\]
Hence by Lemma \ref{lem-convex}, 
\begin{align*}
& \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\sum_{1\le |u|\le N}\mathbb{E}_{u^{-}}\big[\big\|  D_u \big[ M_N^\mathcal{V}\big] \big \|_{\ell^q}^q\big]\Big)^{p/q}\Big]
\\
= &    \|\mathring{W}\|_q^p   \cdot   \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\sum_{1\le |u|\le N}      \Big(  \prod_{j=0}^{|u|-1} W(u|_j)^q \Big)   \cdot  \|\mathcal{V}(I_u)\|_{\ell^q}^q   \Big)^{p/q}\Big] 
\\
\le & \|\mathring{W}\|_q^p   \cdot   \mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big\| \sum_{1\le |u|\le N}    \Big(  \prod_{j=0}^{|u|-1} W(u|_j)^2 \Big)   \cdot  \big| \mathcal{V}(I_u)  \big|^2       \Big\|_{\ell^{q/2}}^{p/2} \Big].
\end{align*}
This ends the proof.

Indeed, by the Fubini Theorem, we have 
 \[

 \]
Therefore,   \eqref{KK-abs} follows from the following: for any finite sequence  $(x_i)_{i}$ in $\ell^{p_1}$, 
 \[
 \big \| \sum_i \epsilon_i x_i\big\|_{L^{p_2} (\Delta; \, \ell^{p_1})} \asymp_{p_1, p_2}  \big \| \sum_i \epsilon_i |x_i|\big\|_{L^{p_2}(\Delta; \, \ell^{p_1})}.
 \]
 By Kahane-Khintchine inequalities \eqref{KK-ineq}, it suffices to show 
 \begin{align}\label{suf-to-prove}
 \big \| \sum_i \epsilon_i x_i\big\|_{L^{p_1}(\Delta; \, \ell^{p_1})} \asymp_{p_1} \big \| \sum_i \epsilon_i |x_i|\big\|_{L^{p_1}(\Delta; \, \ell^{p_1})}.

 Recall the classical  Khintchine inequalities for scalars: for any finite sequence $(a_i)_{i}$ in $\mathbb{C}$, 
 \[

 \]
 The desired equivalence \eqref{suf-to-prove} follows immediately.

For simplifying the notation, for all $u\in \mathcal{A}^*$ with $|u|\ge 1$ and for all $n\ge 1$, we write 
\begin{align}\label{def-Xu}
X(u) : =  \prod_{j=0}^{|u|-1} W(u|_j)^2  \ge 0  \text{\, and \,} Y_n: = \sum_{|u|=n} X(u)
\end{align}
and 
\[
F(s): = \sum_{|u|\ge 1}   X(u)   \cdot    s^{-2 (1 -\alpha)} \cdot  \mathds{1} (s  \ge  b^{|u|}).
\]
Recall the definition \eqref{eqn-def-mnab} for $\mathscr{M}_{n}(W^{(2)})$.  For all $n\ge 1$, we have 
\begin{align}\label{Yn-Mn}
Y_n = \sum_{|u|=n} \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} W(u|_j)^2 =    b  \sum_{|v|=n-1}  \prod_{j=0}^{n-1} W(v|_j)^2 =   b( b \mathbb{E}[W^2])^{n-1}    \mathscr{M}_{n-1}(W^{(2)}).
\end{align}
Then
\begin{align*}
\chi_1 & =   \mathbb{E} \Big[   \Big\{   \sum_{s \ge 1}       \Big(   \sum_{|u|\ge 1}   X(u)   \cdot    s^{-2 (1 -\alpha)} \cdot  \mathds{1} (s \ge b^{|u|}) \Big)^{q/2}  \Big\}^{p/q}\Big]
= \mathbb{E} \Big[   \Big\{     \sum_{l  = 1}^\infty    \sum_{b^{l-1} \le s < b^{l}}  F(s)^{q/2} \Big\}^{p/q}\Big].
\end{align*}
For all integers in the  $b$-adic interval $b^{l-1}\le s < b^l$, we have
\begin{align*}
F(s)\le  T_l: =  & \sum_{|u|\ge 1} X(u)
\cdot   b^{-2(l-1)(1 - \alpha)}  \cdot \mathds{1}(l \ge |u|)  =  \sum_{n=1}^\infty   \underbrace{ Y_n
\cdot   b^{-2(l-1)(1 - \alpha)}  \cdot \mathds{1}(l  \ge n)}_{\text{denoted $T_l(n)$}}. 
\end{align*}
Therefore, 
\begin{align*}
\chi_1 \le  \mathbb{E} \Big[   \Big\{     \sum_{l  = 1}^\infty    \sum_{b^{l-1} \le s < b^{l}}  T_l^{q/2} \Big\}^{p/q}\Big] \le  \mathbb{E} \Big[   \Big\{    \sum_{l  = 1}^\infty    b^l  \cdot T_l^{q/2} \Big\}^{p/q}\Big].
\end{align*}
Since $p/q<1$ and $p/2<1$, by applying twice the inequalities \eqref{2-ele-ineq}, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
\chi_1 & \le \mathbb{E} \Big[  \sum_{l\ge 1}    b^{lp/q}  \cdot T_l^{p/2} \Big]  =  \mathbb{E} \Big[  \sum_{l  \ge 1}    b^{lp/q}  \cdot  \Big(\sum_{n\ge 1} T_l(n)\Big)^{p/2} \Big] 
\\
& \le \mathbb{E} \Big[  \sum_{l  \ge 1}    b^{lp/q}  \cdot  \sum_{n\ge 1} T_l(n)^{p/2}  \Big] =  \sum_{l  \ge 1}   b^{lp/q}  \cdot  \sum_{n\ge 1}   \mathbb{E}[T_l(n)^{p/2}]. 
\end{align*}
Now 
\begin{align*}
 \mathbb{E}[T_l(n)^{p/2}]  &   = \mathbb{E} \Big[   \Big(Y_n
\cdot   b^{-2(l-1)(1 - \alpha)}  \cdot \mathds{1}(l  \ge n)\Big)^{p/2}\Big] = b^{-p (l-1)(1-\alpha)}  \cdot  \mathbb{E}\big [  Y_n^{p/2}\big] \cdot \mathds{1}( l  \ge n). 
\end{align*}
It follows that 
\begin{align*}
\chi_1& \le  \sum_{l  \ge 1}   b^{lp/q}  \cdot  b^{-p (l-1)(1-\alpha)}  \sum_{n\ge 1} \mathbb{E} \big[ Y_n^{p/2}\big] \cdot \mathds{1}( l \ge n)
\\
& \le  b^{p(1-\alpha)} \sum_{n\ge 1}    \mathbb{E} \big[  Y_n^{p/2}\big] \sum_{l\ge 1}  b^{-pl (1-\alpha- \frac{1}{q})}   \cdot \mathds{1}( l  \ge n)
\\
 &\le \frac{b^{p(1-\alpha)}}{1- b^{-p (1-\alpha- \frac{1}{q})} }\sum_{n\ge 1}    \mathbb{E} \big[   Y_n^{p/2}]  b^{-p n (1 - \alpha -  \frac{1}{q})}. 
\end{align*}

Using exactly the same argument as above, we have 
\[
\chi_2\le  \sum_{l  \ge 1}   b^{lp/q}  \cdot  \sum_{n\ge 1}   \mathbb{E}[\widehat{T}_l(n)^{p/2}],
\]
where
\[
\widehat{T}_l(n): =   Y_n \cdot b^{2(l\alpha-n)}  \cdot   \mathds{1}(l-1 \le  n).
\]
Hence
\begin{align*}
\chi_2\le  &  \sum_{n\ge 1}   \mathbb{E}\big[Y_n^{p/2}  \big]\cdot    \sum_{l  \ge 1}    b^{lp/q}  b^{p(l\alpha-n)}        \mathds{1}(l-1\le n)
 \\
\le & \sum_{n\ge 1}   \mathbb{E}\big[Y_n^{p/2}  \big]     \cdot   \frac{b^{p(\alpha + \frac{1}{q})}}{1 - b^{-p(\alpha + \frac{1}{q})}}  \cdot b^{-pn (1 - \alpha - \frac{1}{q})}.
\end{align*}

Finally, by substituting \eqref{Yn-Mn} and \eqref{def-Rn} into the above final inequalities for $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$, we  obtain the desired upper estimate.

nodes.statement: Recall the definition for the function varphi_W: \[ varphi_W(t) = log E[W^t] - (t-1) log b, t>0 \] Clearly, varphi_W is a convex function on (0, infty). Indeed, \[ varphi_W'(t)=fracE[W^tlog W]E[W^t] - log b \] and, by Cauchy-Schwarz's inequality, \[ varphi_W''(t)=fracE[W^t(log W)^2]E[W^t]-(E[W^tlog W])^2(E[W^t])^2ge 0. \] (i). If Ebig[ fracW^2E[W^2] log fracW^2E[W^2]big] le log b, then D_F = 1- log E[W^2]/log b. Hence we need to show E[W^2]> 1 and varphi_W(2) = log E[W^2] - log b <0. The first inequality follows from the assumption that E[W]=1 and Wge 0 is non-constant. We now prove the second inequality. Indeed, in this case, since varphi_W' is increasing, we have varphi_W(2)= varphi_W(2)-varphi_W(1) = int_1^2 varphi_W'(s)ds le varphi_W'(2). Now the condition E[ fracW^2E[W^2] log fracW^2E[W^2]] le log b can be re-written as 2 varphi_W'(2) le varphi_W(2). Consequently, varphi_W(2)le varphi_W'(2) le varphi_W(2)/2 and hence varphi_W(2)le 0. Moreover, if the equality varphi_W(2)=0 holds, then varphi'_W(2) = varphi_W(2) =0 and the inequality becomes an equality. This would imply that varphi_W' is a constant function on the interval [1, 2] and hence \[ 0 = varphi_W'(2)= varphi_W'(1)= E[Wlog W]-log b. \] But this contradicts to the assumption E[Wlog W]<log b. Hence we must have the desired inequality varphi_W(2)<0. (ii). If Ebig[ fracW^2E[W^2] log fracW^2E[W^2]big] > log b, then since E[W^2t] = b^2t-1 e^varphi_W(2t), we need to show D_F= 1 - inf_1/2le tle 1 fraclog E[b^1-tW^2t] t log b = - inf_1/2le tle 1 frac varphi_W(2t)tlog b in (0,1). The inequality D_F>0 follows immediately since varphi_W(1) =0 and by the Kahane's non-degeneracy condition, varphi_W'(1)= E[Wlog W]-log b <0. Finally, the inequality D_F<1 holds if and only if \[ inf_1/2le tle 1 log E[b^1-t W^2t]> 0. \] Assume by contradiction that inf_1/2le tle 1 log E[b^1-t W^2t]=0. Then by continuity of the function tmapsto log E[b^1-t W^2t], there exists t_0in [1/2, 1] such that E[b^1-t_0 W^2t_0] = 1. Clearly, t_0ne 1 since E[W^2]>1. But if t_0in [1/2, 1), then 2t_0ge 1, we have E[W^2t_0] >1 and b^1-t_0>1, contradicts to the assumption E[b^1-t_0 W^2t_0]=1. This completes the proof of D_F<1.

\[

\[

\]
and, by Cauchy-Schwarz's inequality, 
\[

Hence we need to show  $\mathbb{E}[W^2]> 1$ and  $\varphi_W(2) = \log \mathbb{E}[W^2] - \log b <0$. By the definition of the function $\psi$ in \eqref{def-psi} and the relation \eqref{bdary-reg}, we have 
\begin{align*}

\begin{align}\label{big-O}

\[

\end{align*}

\[

\]
where the supremum ranges over all finite subsets  $F\subset \mathbb{N}$.  In particular,  given $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$,  the limit 
\[
\sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} e^{-\beta x_i}\widehat{\mu}^{(i)}_\infty(1) = \lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^N e^{-\beta x_i}\widehat{\mu}^{(i)}_\infty(1)

For  $s\in \mathbb{N}$,  by definition one has $\widehat{\mu}_0(s)=0$ and 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-m-differ-s}
\widehat{\mu}_{m}(s)-\widehat{\mu}_{m-1}(s)=\sum_{|u|=m}  \Big(\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} W(u|_j)\Big) \mathring{W}(u) \cdot \int_{I_u} e^{-i2\pi s x}dx , \quad \forall m \in \mathbb{N},
\end{align}
Notice that if $|u|\leq n$, one has $ \int_{I_u} e^{i2\pi b^n x}dx=0$ and hence 
\[
\widehat{\mu}_{n}\left(b^n\right) =\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\widehat{\mu}_{m}\left(b^n\right)-\widehat{\mu}_{m-1}\left(b^n\right)\right) =0 .
\]
It follows that 
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^n\right) & =\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^n\right)-\widehat{\mu}_{n}\left(b^n\right) 
 =\sum_{m=n+1}^{\infty}\left(\widehat{\mu}_{m}\left(b^n\right)-\widehat{\mu}_{m-1}\left(b^n\right)\right) \\
&=\sum_{m=n+1}^{\infty} \,\,\sum_{|u|=m} \Big(\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} W(u|_j)\Big) \mathring{W}(u) \cdot \int_{I_u} e^{-i 2 \pi b^n x} d x. 
\end{align*}
Note that each $u$ with $|u|=m\ge n+1$ can be uniquely written as  $u= vw$ such that  $|v|=n$ and $|w|=m-n$.  For any $n+1\le j \le m-1$, we have 
\[
(vw)|_j = v (w|_{j-n}) = v  \cdot w|_{j-n}. 
\]
Therefore, by using the elementary identity 
\[
\sum_{|u|=m}   f(u) =     \sum_{|v|=n} \sum_{|w|= m-n} f(vw)
\]
and writing  
\[
\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} W(u|_j)    = \prod_{j=0}^{m-1} W((vw)|_j)  = \Big(\prod_{j=0}^{n} W(v|_j)\Big) \cdot \Big(\prod_{l=1}^{m-n-1} W(v \cdot w|_l)\Big),
\]
we obtain 
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^n\right)  &= \sum_{m=n+1}^{\infty} \,\,\sum_{|v|=n} \sum_{|w|= m-n}    \Big(\prod_{j=0}^{n} W(v|_j)\Big) \cdot \Big(\prod_{l=1}^{m-n-1} W(v\cdot w|_l)\Big)      \mathring{W}(vw) \cdot \int_{I_{vw}} e^{-i 2 \pi b^n x} d x\\
&=\sum_{|v|=n}\Big(\prod_{j=0}^{n} W(v|_j)\Big) \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{|w|=k} \Big( \prod_{l=1}^{k-1} W( v\cdot w|_l)  \Big) \mathring{W}(vw) \int_{I_{vw}} e^{-i 2 \pi b^n x} d x,
\end{align*}
where we used the convention (for $k=1$)
\[
 \prod_{l=1}^{k-1} W( v\cdot w|_l)  = 1. 
\]
By a direct computation,  for $|v|=n$,  we have 
\[
\int_{I_{vw}} e^{i 2 \pi b^n x} d x = b^{-n} \int_{I_w} e^{-i 2\pi x} dx. 
\]
Hence
\begin{align*}
\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^n\right) 
&= \frac{1}{b^n}\sum_{|v|=n}\Big(\prod_{j=0}^{n} W(v|_j)\Big) \cdot  \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{|w|=k} \Big( \prod_{l=1}^{k-1} W( v\cdot w|_l)  \Big) \mathring{W}(vw) \int_{I_{w}} e^{-i 2 \pi x} d x}_{\text{denoted as $\widehat{\mu}_\infty^{(v)}(1)$}}.
\end{align*}
Clearly,  $\{\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(v)}(1): |v|=n\}$  are i.i.d. copies of $\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}(1)$ and are independent of the sigma-algebra $\mathscr{F}_{n}=\sigma\{W(u)| 1\leq |u|\leq n\}$. This completes the proof.

\[
 \big\{\sqrt{Y(u)}  \cdot \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)\big\}_{|u|=n}
\]
with conditional covariance matrix given by \eqref{eqn-cov-conditional}. Apparently, 
\[
\mathrm{Cov}\Big[b^{\frac{n D_F}{2}}\cdot \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}(b^n)\big| \mathscr{F}_{n}\Big]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{a.s.}    \varrho \mathscr{M}_\infty(W^{(2)})

1/2 &0\\
0&1/2 \\
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

We shall check the conditional  Lindeberg-Feller condition in Proposition~\ref{Prop-c-clt}. 
In other words, we need to show that,  for any $\varepsilon>0$, the following holds:
 \begin{align}\label{eqn-CLT-feller}
\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \sum_{|u|=n} \mathbb{E}[Y(u) |\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)|^2\mathds{1}(Y(u) |\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)|^2>\varepsilon)|\mathscr{F}_n]=0.
 \end{align}
Set 
 \begin{align}\label{eqn-CLT-sigma}
\sigma(x): =\mathbb{E}\big[|\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}(1)|^2 \mathds{1}(|\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}(1)|^2>x)\big], \quad \forall x \geqslant 0.
\end{align}

\sigma(x)\downarrow 0 \quad \text{as $x\uparrow \infty $ }.
\end{align}

\[

\]

\[

\]

Recall the Kahane's $L^p$-criterion: If $1<p<\infty$, then  $\mathbb{E}[\mu_\infty([0,1])^p]<\infty$ if and only if $\mathbb{E}[W^p]<b^{p-1}$. Note that, in the boundary case,  
\[
\mathbb{E}[W^t]<b^{t-1} \Longleftrightarrow \frac{\psi(t \beta)}{t\beta} < \frac{\psi(\beta)}{\beta}. 
\]
Since $\psi(1)= 0, \psi(\beta)> 0$ and  $\psi$ is continuous,  one can find $p\in (\frac{1}{\beta}, 2]$ with
$
\frac{\psi(p \beta)}{p\beta} < \frac{\psi(\beta)}{\beta}
$
and hence 
$
\mathbb{E}[W^p]<b^{p-1}. 
$
Now we fix this exponent $p\in (1/\beta, 2]$.  First of all, we have 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-finite-p-moment}
\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^p]  \le \mathbb{E}[\mu_\infty ([0,1])^p ]<\infty.
\end{align}
To prove $\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^p]> 0$, we may apply Bourgain-Stein inequality as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm-precise}.   For avoiding the repetition of the same lines of arguments, here,  we derive $\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^p]> 0$ from  Theorem~\ref{thm-precise}. More precisely,  let $\mathcal{V}: \mathfrak{B}^b \rightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the scalar complex measure defined by 
\[
\mathcal{V}(I_u):=\int_{I_u} e^{-i 2\pi x}dx. 
\]
Recall the definition   \eqref{def-mart} of $Q_n\mathcal{V}([0,1])$: 
\[
Q_n\mathcal{V} ([0,1]) = \sum_{|u|=n}  \Big(\prod_{j=0}^n W(u|_j)\Big) \cdot \mathcal{V}(I_u)=\widehat{\mu}_n(1), \quad n\ge 1. 
\] 
Set
\begin{align*}
\chi(\mathcal{V}, W, p): =   \mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big| \sum_{|u|\ge 1}    \Big(  \prod_{j=0}^{|u|-1} W(u|_j)^2 \Big)   \cdot  \big| \mathcal{V}(I_u)  \big|^2       \Big|^{p/2} \Big]>0.
\end{align*}
Then Theorem~\ref{thm-precise} implies that 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^p]=\lim_{n \rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_n(1)|^p] =\limsup_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_n(1)|^p] \geq C_p   \|\mathring{W}\|_1^p\cdot    \chi(\mathcal{V}, W, p)>0.   
\end{align*} 




We now proceed to the proof of the second part of the lemma. Using \eqref{eqn-psi-t-star}, we obtain
\[
\mathbb{E}\Big[\big| b^{\frac{n D_F}{2}}   n^{\frac{3}{2}\beta} \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^n\right)\big|^{p\gamma}\Big] =   \mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|     \sum_{|u|=n} e^{-\beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)  \Big|^{p\gamma}   \Big]. 
\]
Since $0< \gamma< \frac{1}{p\beta}< 1$,  by Jensen's inequality 
\[
\mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|     \sum_{|u|=n} e^{-\beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)  \Big|^{p\gamma}   \Big|\mathscr{F}_n\Big]  \le   \Big( \mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|     \sum_{|u|=n} e^{-\beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)  \Big|^{p}   \Big|\mathscr{F}_n\Big] \Big)^\gamma.
\]
Now since  $1< \frac{1}{\beta}< p\le 2$, we can apply Burkholder's martingale  inequality  (since, conditioned on $\mathscr{F}_n$, the sequence  $(\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1))_{|u|=n}$ are i.i.d. and mean zero) and obtain 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|     \sum_{|u|=n} e^{-\beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)  \Big|^{p}   \Big|\mathscr{F}_n\Big]   \lesssim_p   \mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|     \sum_{|u|=n} e^{-2 \beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}|\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)|^2  \Big|^{\frac{p}{2}}   \Big|\mathscr{F}_n\Big]. 
\end{align*}
Thus, since $p/2\le 1$,  by applying \eqref{2-ele-ineq}, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|     \sum_{|u|=n} e^{-\beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)  \Big|^{p}   \Big|\mathscr{F}_n\Big]   & \lesssim_p   \mathbb{E}\Big[ \Big|     \sum_{|u|=n} e^{- p \beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}|\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)|^{p}  \Big|\mathscr{F}_n\Big] 
\\
& =        \sum_{|u|=n} e^{- p \beta ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )} \mathbb{E}[ |\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(u)}(1)|^{p}].  
\end{align*}
Therefore, we arrive at 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\Big[\big| b^{\frac{n D_F}{2}}   n^{\frac{3}{2}\beta} \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^n\right)\big|^{p\gamma}\Big]\lesssim_p  \mathbb{E}\Big[\Big(\sum_{|u|=n} e^{-\beta p ( V(u)-\frac{3}{2}\log n )}\Big)^{\gamma}\Big]\,\,\cdot(\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}(1)|^p])^\gamma.
\end{align*}
Since   $\beta p>1$ and $\gamma<\frac{1}{\beta p}$, by  \eqref{s-m-asymp} and  \eqref{eqn-finite-p-moment}, 
\[
\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}^+}\mathbb{E}\Big[\big| b^{\frac{n D_F}{2}}   n^{\frac{3}{2}\beta} \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}\left(b^n\right) \big|^{p\gamma}\Big]<\infty.
\]
This completes the proof.

The proof of Proposition~\ref{thm-non-cri-super-critical} is divided into three steps.

{\flushleft \it Step 1: Tightness and limit.}
Lemma~\ref{lemma-tightness} implies  the tightness of the family 
\[
\Big\{ b^{\frac{n D_F}{2}}   n^{\frac{3}{2}\beta} \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}(b^{n})  : n\in \mathbb{N}\Big\}. 
\]
Therefore,  by using the similar arguments as \cite[Theorem 2.5]{Iksanov} and recalling the random variable $\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})$ given by \eqref{root-n-M},  we have the convergence in distribution: 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-limit-exists-s}
   b^{\frac{n D_F}{2}}   n^{\frac{3}{2}\beta} \widehat{\mu}_{\infty}(b^{n})     \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{d}       \mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})^\beta   \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} e^{-\beta x_i}\widehat{\mu}^{(i)}_\infty(1),
\end{align}
where $(x_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ is the  point process  $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$ in \eqref{eqn-z-infinity-s},  $\{\widehat{\mu}^{(i)}_\infty(1)\}_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ are i.i.d. copies of $\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)$  independent of $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$ and    $\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})$ is independent of   $(\mathcal{Z}_\infty, \{\widehat{\mu}^{(i)}_\infty(1)\}_{i\in \mathbb{N}})$. 


{\flushleft \it Step 2: Non-trivial limit.} We shall show that the limit in \eqref{eqn-limit-exists-s} is non-trivial (not identically zero).  Indeed,  let  $p\in (1/\beta,2]$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lemma-tightness}. Since the point process $\mathcal{Z}_\infty=(x_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ and the sequence of random variables $(\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(i)} (1) )_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ are independent,  Burkholder's  inequality implies that 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\Big[\big|\sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} e^{-\beta x_i}\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(i)} (1) \big|^p\mid \mathcal{Z}_\infty \Big]& \gtrsim_p \mathbb{E}\Big[\big(\sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} e^{-2\beta x_i}|\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(i)} (1) |^2\big)^{\frac{p}{2}}\mid \mathcal{Z}_\infty \Big]\geq e^{-p\beta x_1}\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(1)|^p].
\end{align*}
Since  the point process   $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$ is non-trivial, 
we have 
\[
\mathbb{E}\Big[\big|\sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} e^{-\beta x_i}\widehat{\mu}_{\infty}^{(i)} (1) \big|^p\Big]>0.
\]

{\flushleft \it Step 3: Stable law.}    
By \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Mad}, under $\mathbb{P}^*$, the point process $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$ in \eqref{eqn-z-infinity-s} has the following description:  Take the $\mathbb{P}^*$-a.s. limit of derivative martingale 
\[
\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{|u|=n} V(u) e^{-V(u)}
\] 
with 
\[
 \mathbb{P}^*(\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})\in(0,\infty))=1.
\]
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be an independent Poisson point process on the whole line $\mathbb{R}$ whose intensity measure is given by  $\lambda\mathrm{e}^y \mathrm{~d} y$ for some $\lambda>0$. For each atom $y$ of $\mathcal{P}$, we attach a point process $\mathcal{Q}^{(y)}$, where $\mathcal{Q}^{(y)}$ are independent copies  (given $\mathcal{P}$) of a certain point process $\mathcal{Q}$.  Denote $\mathcal{P}=\{y_i: i\in\mathbb{N}\}$ and $\mathcal{Q}^{(y_i)}=\{z_j^{(i)}: i\in \mathbb{N}\}$, which are all assumed to be independent of $\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})$.   Then 
\[
\mathcal{Z}_\infty \stackrel{d}{=}\{y_i+z_j^{(i)} - \log \mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)}): i, j\in\mathbb{N}\}.
\]
It follows that 
\[
X:=       \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}} e^{-\beta x_i}   \mathrm{Re}( \widehat{\mu}^{(i)}_\infty(1) )  \stackrel{d}{=}  \mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})^\beta  \underbrace{ \sum_{i, j\in\mathbb{N}}e^{-\beta (y_i+z_j^{(i)})}\mathrm{Re}(\widehat{\mu}^{(i, j)}_\infty(1))}_{\text{denoted as $\widetilde{X}$}}=\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})^\beta \sum_{i\in \mathbb{N}}e^{-\beta y_i} R_i
\]
 with 
 \[
 R_i=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{N}} e^{-\beta z_j^{(i)}}\mathrm{Re}(\widehat{\mu}^{(i, j)}_\infty(1)). 
\]
Note that, given $\mathcal{Z}_\infty$,  both summations for $\widetilde{X}$ and   $R_i$ are  well-defined (see Lemma \ref{lem-partition}  below and are understood as in \eqref{def-Spk}). 

The transformed  point process  $\widehat{\mathcal{P}}=\{\widehat{y}_i=e^{-\beta y_i}: i\in \mathbb{N}\}$ of $\mathcal{P}$  is  a Poisson point process on $\mathbb{R}_+$ with new intensity measure given by 
\[
\rho(dy)=\frac{\lambda}{\beta}y^{-1-\frac{1}{\beta}}  \mathds{1}(y>0) dy.
\]
Thus we can write 
  \[
  \widetilde{X}= \sum_{\widehat{y}_i\in \widehat{\mathcal{P}}}\widehat{y}_i R_i  \text{\, and \,} X \overset{d}{=} \mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})^\beta\widetilde{X},
  \]
   where $\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)})$ and $\widetilde{X}$ are independent, and $(R_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ are i.i.d. copies of a random variable $R$ and the sum is understood as a   martingale limit (given $\widehat{\mathcal{P}}$). 

For any $\varepsilon>0$, consider the truncated sum
\[
\widetilde{X}_\varepsilon=\sum_{\widehat{y}_i\in \widehat{\mathcal{P}}}\mathds{1}(\widehat{y}_i\ge \varepsilon)\widehat{y}_i R_i.
\]
Almost surely, $\widetilde{X}_\varepsilon$ is a  finite sum. 
 Under $\mathbb{P}^*$,  the Fourier transform of $\widetilde{X}_\varepsilon$  is given by 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}^*[\exp( it \widetilde{X}_\varepsilon)]&=\mathbb{E}^*\Big[\prod_{\widehat{y}_i \in \widehat{\mathcal{P}} \cap [\varepsilon, \infty)}   \exp (i t  \widehat{y}_i R_i)   \Big] =\mathbb{E}^*\Big [   \mathbb{E}^* \Big[ \prod_{\widehat{y}_i \in \widehat{\mathcal{P}} \cap [\varepsilon, \infty)}   \exp (i t \widehat{y}_i R_i)    \Big| \widehat{\mathcal{P}} \Big] \Big]. 
\end{align*}
Let  $f_R(t): = \mathbb{E}^*[\exp(itR)]$ be the Fourier transform of the random variable $R$. Then by the  independence between  $(R_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal{P}}$,
\[
 \mathbb{E}^* \Big[ \prod_{\widehat{y}_i \in \widehat{\mathcal{P}} \cap [\varepsilon, \infty)}   \exp (i t \widehat{y}_i R_i)    \Big| \widehat{\mathcal{P}} \Big] =  \prod_{\widehat{y}_i \in \widehat{\mathcal{P}} \cap [\varepsilon, \infty)}      f_R (t\widehat{y}_i). 
\]
Therefore, by the Bogoliubov functional (or the Laplace transform) of the Poisson point process (see \cite[Section 3.2]{Kingman}), we have 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}^*[\exp( it\widetilde{X}_\varepsilon)] & =  \mathbb{E}^*\Big[  \prod_{\widehat{y}_i \in \widehat{\mathcal{P}} \cap [\varepsilon, \infty)}      f_R (t\widehat{y}_i)\Big]
\\
&  =\exp\Big(\int_{\varepsilon}^\infty \big(f_R(ty)-1\big)  \frac{\lambda dy}{ \beta y^{1+1/\beta}}\Big) 
\\
 &  = \exp\Big({|t|^{\frac{1}{\beta}}} \int_{ |t| \varepsilon}^\infty  (f_R( \mathrm{sgn}(t) \cdot y)-1) \frac{\lambda dy}{\beta y^{1+1/\beta}}\Big),
\end{align*}
where in the last step, we used the  change of variable $|t|y \to y$.  
By Dominated Convergence Theorem, 
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}  \mathbb{E}^*[\exp( it \widetilde{X}_\varepsilon)] =  \mathbb{E}^*[\exp( it\widetilde{X})]. 
\]
It follows that the following limit exists 
\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0} \int_{ |t| \varepsilon}^\infty  (f_R( \mathrm{sgn}(t)\cdot y)-1) \frac{\lambda dy}{\beta y^{1+1/\beta}} =  \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0} \int_{\varepsilon}^\infty  (f_R( \mathrm{sgn}(t) \cdot y)-1) \frac{\lambda dy}{\beta y^{1+1/\beta}}. 
\]
Consequently, 
\[
\mathbb{E}^*[\exp( it\widetilde{X})] = \exp\big( (c_1  + i \mathrm{sgn}(t) c_2)  |t|^{\frac{1}{\beta}}\big)
\]
and 
\[
 \mathbb{E}^*[\exp( it X)] =
\mathbb{E}^*\big[ \exp\big( (c_1  + i \mathrm{sgn}(t) c_2)  |t|^{\frac{1}{\beta}}\mathscr{D}_\infty(W^{(2)}) \big)\big],
\]
where 
\begin{align}\label{c-1}
c_1  =  \int_{0}^\infty  ( \mathbb{E}^*[\cos (Ry) ]  -1) \frac{\lambda dy}{\beta y^{1+1/\beta}} <0
\end{align}
and 
\begin{align}\label{c-2}
c_2  =   \lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}   \int_{\varepsilon}^\infty \mathbb{E}^*[\sin (Ry) ]   \frac{\lambda dy}{\beta y^{1+1/\beta}}. 
\end{align}
In other words, 
\[
\mathbb{E}^*[\exp( it\widetilde{X})] = \exp\big( -c  (1 + i \mathrm{sgn}(t) c')  |t|^{\frac{1}{\beta}}\big) \quad \text{with $c> 0$}.  
\]
Hence, under $\mathbb{P}^*$, the random variable  $\widetilde{X}$ has a $\frac{1}{\beta}$-stable law.  The desired equality \eqref{zero-prob} follows since  any stable law is  continuous.

\label{lemma-cov-law-con-two}
Let $(X_n)_{n\geq 1}$  and $X_\infty$ be  complex random variables on some probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$. Assume that  $E\in\mathcal{F} $ satisfies $\mathbb{P}(E)=\mathbb{P}(X_\infty\neq 0)\in (0,1)$ and $X_n=0$ on $E^c$ for any $n\geq 1$ . 
If 
\[
X_n\xrightarrow[n\rightarrow\infty]{d} X_\infty,
\]
then the following conditioned convergence in distribution holds:
\[
\mathcal{L}(X_n\mid E)\xrightarrow[]{n\rightarrow\infty} \mathcal{L}(X_\infty|X_\infty\neq 0).
\]

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma \ref{lem-trans-coef}
nodes.statement: By Proposition~, if |widehatmu(n)| = O(n^-kappa) with kappa in (0, 1] as Nni ntoinfty, then \[ |widehatmu_0(n)| = O(n^-kappa log n) \, and \, |widehatmu_1(n)| = O(n^-kappa log n), \] where mu_0 = mu|_[0,1/2) and mu_1= mu|_[1/2, 1] are the restrictions of mu on two sub-intervals. Now since both supp(mu_0) and supp(mu_1) are contained in a sub-interval of length strictly less than 1, we can apply to mu_0 and mu_1 respectively and obtain \[ |mu(zeta)| le |mu_0(zeta)| + |mu_1(zeta)| = O big( |zeta|^-kappa log (|zeta|)big) as Rni zeta to infty. \] The above argument shows that \[ sup\D in[0,1]: |widehatmu_infty(zeta)|^2 = O(|zeta|^-D) \ le sup \ D in [0,1): |widehatmu(n)|^2 = O(n^-D) \. \] The converse inequality is trivial. Hence we complete the proof of the lemma.

By Proposition~\ref{lem-Fdecay},  if $|\widehat{\mu}(n)|  = O(n^{-\kappa})$ with $\kappa \in (0, 1]$ as $\mathbb{N}\ni n\to\infty$, then 
\[
|\widehat{\mu}_0(n)|  = O(n^{-\kappa} \log n) \text{\, and \,}  |\widehat{\mu}_1(n)| = O(n^{-\kappa} \log n),
\]
where $\mu_0 = \mu|_{[0,1/2)}$ and $\mu_1= \mu|_{[1/2, 1]}$ are the restrictions of $\mu$ on two sub-intervals. Now since both $\mathrm{supp}(\mu_0)$ and $\mathrm{supp}(\mu_1)$ are contained in a sub-interval of length strictly less than $1$,  we can apply \cite[Chapter 17, Lemma 1]{Kahane-book} to $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$ respectively and obtain 
\[
\text{$|\mu(\zeta)| \le    |\mu_0(\zeta)|  + |\mu_1(\zeta)|   = O  \big( |\zeta|^{-\kappa} \log (|\zeta|)\big)$ as $\mathbb{R}\ni \zeta \to \infty$.}
\]
The above argument shows that 
\[
 \sup\{D \in[0,1]:   |\widehat{\mu}_\infty(\zeta)|^2 = O(|\zeta|^{-D}) \}     \le    \sup \{ D \in [0,1):     |\widehat{\mu}(n)|^2  = O(n^{-D})   \}.
\]
The converse inequality is trivial. Hence we complete the proof of the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary \ref{cor-series-dim}
nodes.statement: Let mu be a finite positive Borel measure on [0,1]. By Lemma , we have \[ dim_F(mu) = sup \ D in [0,1): |widehatmu(n)|^2 = O(n^-D) \. \] Set \[ D'(mu) := sup Big\D in [0,1): sum_nge 1 | n^fracD2 cdot widehatmu(n)|^q <infty for some q>2 Big\. \] If 0le D<1 is such that |widehatmu(n)|^2 = O(n^-D). Then for any varepsilonin (0,1) and q>2/varepsilon>2, we have \[ sum_nge 1 | n^fracD-varepsilon2 cdot widehatmu(n)|^q le sup_nin N (n^D |widehatmu(n)|^2)^q/2 cdot sum_nge 1 n^- fracvarepsilon q2<infty. \] Hence D-varepsilonle D'(mu). Since Dle dim_F(mu) and varepsilon>0 are arbitrary, we obtain dim_F(mu)le D'(mu). The converse inequality is proved similarly.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel  measure on $[0,1]$.  By Lemma \ref{lem-trans-coef}, we have 
\[
\dim_F(\mu) =  \sup \{ D \in [0,1):     |\widehat{\mu}(n)|^2  = O(n^{-D})   \}.
\]
Set
 \[
D'(\mu) := \sup \Big\{D \in [0,1):    \text{$  \sum_{n\ge 1 } | n^{\frac{D}{2}}  \cdot \widehat{\mu}(n)|^q <\infty$ for some $q>2$}    \Big\}. 
\]
If $0\le D<1$ is such that  
$
 |\widehat{\mu}(n)|^2  = O(n^{-D}). $ Then for any $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and $q>2/\varepsilon>2$, we have  
 \[
  \sum_{n\ge 1 } | n^{\frac{D-\varepsilon}{2}}  \cdot \widehat{\mu}(n)|^q    \le \sup_{n\in \mathbb{N}} (n^D |\widehat{\mu}(n)|^2)^{q/2}    \cdot \sum_{n\ge 1} n^{- \frac{\varepsilon q}{2}}<\infty. 
   \]
Hence  $D-\varepsilon\le D'(\mu)$. Since $D\le \dim_F(\mu)$ and $\varepsilon>0$ are arbitrary, we obtain $\dim_F(\mu)\le D'(\mu)$.  The converse inequality is proved similarly.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem \ref{thm-fourier}
nodes.statement: Recall the definition of tau_c(mu_infty): \[ tau_c(mu_infty): = sup Big\tau in R: sum_nge 1 | n^tau cdot widehatmu_infty(n)|^q<infty \, for some q>2 Big\. \] Recall also the definition alpha_c : \[ alpha_c = sup Big\alpha in R: Big(EBig[ Big\ sum_n ge 1 big| n^alpha cdot widehatmu_infty(n)big|^q Big\^fracpqBig] Big)^frac1p <infty \, for some 1<p<2<q<infty Big\. \] Clearly, \[ tau_c(mu_infty) ge alpha_c a.s. \] On the other hand, as a consequence of Corollary , almost surely on \mu_infty ne 0\, we have the equality \[ dim_F(mu_infty) = min( 2 tau_c(mu_infty), 1). \] By Proposition , under the assumptions of Theorem , we have \[ alpha_cge D_F/2. \] Moreover, by Lemma , D_Fin (0,1). Consequently, almost surely on \mu_infty ne 0\, \[ dim_F(mu_infty) = min(2 tau_c(mu_infty), 1) ge min(2 alpha_c, 1) ge min( D_F, 1) = D_F a.s. \] Finally, by Proposition , almost surely on \mu_infty ne 0\, \[ dim_F(mu_infty) le D_F + frac1k \] for any kin N and hence dim_F(mu_infty) le D_F. This completes the proof of the desired exact Fourier dimension formula dim_F(mu_infty) = D_F.

Recall the definition \eqref{def-tau-c} of $\tau_c(\mu_\infty)$:
\[
\tau_c(\mu_\infty): =  \sup \Big\{\tau \in \mathbb{R}: \sum_{n\ge 1} | n^{\tau}  \cdot \widehat{\mu}_\infty(n)|^q<\infty \text{\, for some $q>2$} \Big\}. 
\]
Recall also the definition   \eqref{def-a-c}  $\alpha_c$ :
\[
\alpha_c =  \sup \Big\{\alpha \in \mathbb{R}:    \Big(\mathbb{E}\Big[  \Big\{ \sum_{n \ge 1}    \big| n^{\alpha} \cdot \widehat{\mu}_\infty(n)\big|^q  \Big\}^{\frac{p}{q}}\Big] \Big)^{\frac{1}{p}}  <\infty \text{\, for some $1<p<2<q<\infty$} \Big\}.
\]
Clearly, 
\[
\tau_c(\mu_\infty) \ge \alpha_c \quad a.s. 
\]
On the other hand, as a consequence of Corollary \ref{cor-series-dim},   almost surely on $\{\mu_\infty \ne 0\}$, we have  the equality 
\[
\dim_F(\mu_\infty) = \min( 2 \tau_c(\mu_\infty), 1).
\]
By Proposition \ref{prop-sq-3case}, under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{thm-fourier}, we have 
\[
\alpha_c\ge D_F/2. 
\]
Moreover, by Lemma \ref{lem-DF}, $D_F\in (0,1)$. Consequently,  almost surely on $\{\mu_\infty \ne 0\}$,
\[
\dim_F(\mu_\infty)   = \min(2 \tau_c(\mu_\infty), 1)  \ge    \min(2 \alpha_c, 1) \ge \min( D_F, 1) = D_F \quad a.s. 
\]


Finally, by Proposition \ref{prop-to-infty},  almost surely on $\{\mu_\infty \ne 0\}$, 
\[
\dim_F(\mu_\infty) \le D_F + \frac{1}{k}
\]
 for any $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and hence  
$
\dim_F(\mu_\infty) \le D_F. 
$
This completes the proof of the desired exact Fourier dimension formula $\dim_F(\mu_\infty) = D_F$.

\[
\begin{cases}
1<p< \min(2, 1 + \delta)\le     2\le q<\infty,
\vspace{2mm}
\\

\vspace{2mm}
\\
\displaystyle\frac{\log \mathbb{E}[W^p]}{\log b}  < (\tau(p, q, \alpha)- 1) \underline{\dim}_{\tau(p, q, \alpha)}(\nu).
\end{cases}
\]
Then we shall show that, under the assumption \eqref{W-ass-Fdim},   almost surely on $\{Q\nu\ne 0\}$, 
\[
\dim_F(Q\nu)\ge   2 \eta_W(\nu) > 0.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{prop-full}
Let $\nu$ be a  Borel probability measure on $[0,1]$ satisfying the condition \eqref{W-ass-Fdim}.  Assume that $W\in L^{1+\delta}(\mathbb{P})$ for a positive $\delta>0$.   Then  $Q$ acts fully on $\nu$, namely, 
\[
Q_n\nu([0,1])=  \mathbb{E}_n[Q\nu([0,1])] \quad a.s. \quad \text{for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$}.
\]

Take the vector measure $\mathcal{V}$ in Corollary \ref{cor-HM-comp} to be the probability measure $\nu$ on $[0,1]$ and by the equality \eqref{H=pdim}, we get

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{lem-gen-measure}
Let $\nu$ be a  Borel probability measure on $[0,1]$.  Assume that there exist $\kappa\in (0,1]$ and $c>0$ such that 
\[
|\widehat{\nu}(l)|\le  \frac{c}{|l|^{\kappa}} \quad \text{for all $l\in \mathbb{Z}^* = \mathbb{Z}\setminus \{0\}$}.
\]
Then for any $0< \alpha < \kappa$ and  $q>(\kappa- \alpha)^{-1}$, the growth rate function $H_{\mathcal{V}}$ of the vector measure $\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{V}_{\alpha, q}$ defined in \eqref{def-Valpha} has the upper estimate: 
\begin{align}\label{HV-upper}
H_{\mathcal{V}}(p) \le         p-1 -  (\tau(\alpha, p, q) - 1) \underline{\dim}_{\tau(\alpha, p, q)}(\nu)  \quad \text{for all $p> \frac{q\kappa}{q(\kappa - \alpha) -1}$},
\end{align}
where
\[
\tau(\alpha,p, q) = p \frac{q(\kappa-\alpha) - 1}{q \kappa}>1.
\]

Note that  from the proof of  Lemma~\ref{lemma-jihi}, if $\mathbb{E}[W^2]<b$, then 
for any $k \in\mathbb{N}$, one has
\begin{align}\label{eqn-esdt}
\mathbb{E}[|\widehat{\mu}_\infty(k)|^2]=\frac{\mathrm{Var}(W)}{\mathbb{E}[W^2]}\sum_{n=1}^\infty \big(b\mathbb{E}[W^2]\big)^{n}\Big|\frac{e^{i2\pi k b^{-n}}-1}{2\pi k}\Big|^2.
\end{align}
Denote by  $T(k,n):=\frac{\big|e^{i2\pi  k b^{-n}}-1\big|^2}{4\pi k^2}$ and use $|e^{i2\pi x}-1|\asymp |x|$ for $|x|\leq 1$,
one obtains   
\begin{align*}
\sum_{n=1}^\infty(b\mathbb{E}[W^2])^n\,T(k,n)
=& \sum_{1\leq n\leq \lceil \log_b k \rceil}(b\mathbb{E}[W^2])^n\,T(k,n)+\sum_{n\geq \lceil \log_b k \rceil +1} (b\mathbb{E}[W^2])^n\,T(k,n)\\
\leq &\frac{1}{2\pi k ^2}\sum_{1\leq n\leq \lceil \log_b k \rceil}(b\mathbb{E}[W^2])^n+C_1 \sum_{n\geq \lceil \log_b k \rceil +1} \big(\frac{\mathbb{E}[W^2]}{b}\big)^n\\
\leq& C_2 k^{-2}(b\mathbb{E}[W^2])^{\lceil \log_b k \rceil}+C_3 \big(\frac{\mathbb{E}[W^2]}{b}\big)^{\lceil \log_b k \rceil +1}\\
\leq&  C_2 k ^{-2}(b\mathbb{E}[W^2])^{\log_b k }+C_3 \big(\frac{\mathbb{E}[W^2]}{b}\big)^{\log_b k }\\
=&  C \big(\frac{\mathbb{E}[W^2]}{b}\big)^{\log_b k } = C k^{-\big(1-\frac{\log \mathbb{E}[W^2]}{\log b}\big)},
\end{align*}
where   $C_1$ is an  absolute constant and $C_2,C_3, C$ are constants depending only on $b$ and $\mathbb{E}[W^2]$.  

On the other hand, we have
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{n=1}^\infty(b\mathbb{E}[W^2])^n\,T(k,n)
\geq  \sum_{n\geq \lceil \log_b k \rceil } \big(\frac{\mathbb{E}[W^2]}{b}\big)^n\geq C_4 \big(\frac{\mathbb{E}[W^2]}{b}\big)^{\log_b k }=C_4 k^{-\big(1-\frac{\log \mathbb{E}[W^2]}{\log b}\big)},
\end{align*}
where $C_4$ is a constant depending only on $\mathbb{E}[W^2]$ and $b$. Therefore we get the desired relation \eqref{eqn-rela-sd}.

Recall the definition \eqref{def-H-mart} of $T_n^\mathcal{V}$. Here we have 
\[
T_n : =   b^n \sum_{|u|=n}      \Big(  s^\alpha   \int_{I_u}  e^{-i 2 \pi s t}dt\Big)_{s \ge 1}  \mathds{1}_{I_u}.
\]
By \eqref{V-exp}, we have 
\[
\|T_n\|^p_{L^p(\ell^q)} = \frac{b^{np}}{2^p \pi^p} \Big( \underbrace{ \sum_{s=1}^\infty     s^{-(1-\alpha)q}  | e^{i 2 \pi sb^{-n}} - 1 |^q}_{\text{denoted $\Sigma_n$}}\Big)^{p/q}. 
\]
By regrouping all $s$ according to their congruent classes in $\mathbb{Z}/b^n\mathbb{Z}$, we have 
\begin{align*}
\Sigma_n &= \sum_{k=1}^{b^n}     \sum_{l=0}^\infty (k+b^n l )^{-(1-\alpha)q} \cdot | e^{i 2 \pi (k+b^nl)b^{-n}} - 1 |^q 
\\
& = \sum_{k=1}^{b^n} | e^{i 2 \pi k b^{-n}} - 1 |^q  \sum_{l=0}^\infty (k+b^n l)^{-(1-\alpha)q}
\\
&= \underbrace{\sum_{k=1}^{b^n} | e^{i 2 \pi k b^{-n}} - 1 |^q  k^{-(1-\alpha)q} }_{\text{denoted $\Sigma_n'$}}  + \underbrace{ \sum_{k=1}^{b^n} | e^{i 2 \pi k b^{-n}} - 1 |^q  \sum_{l=1}^\infty (k+b^n l)^{-(1-\alpha)q}}_{\text{denoted $\Sigma_n''$}}.
\end{align*}
By using the limit of Riemann sum of a continuous function (here the assumption $\alpha\in [0,1)$ is used), we have 
\begin{align*}
\lim_{n\to\infty} b^{n [ -1+ (1-\alpha)q]}   \Sigma_n' 
= \int_0^1   \Big|\frac{ e^{i 2 \pi t } - 1}{t^{1-\alpha}} \Big|^q dt  = :c_1(\alpha, q)\in (0,\infty).
\end{align*}
For the term $\Sigma_n''$, note that by assumption,  we have $q(1-\alpha)>1$ and 
\begin{align*}
  \Sigma_n''& \le   \sum_{k=1}^{b^n} | e^{i 2 \pi k b^{-n}} - 1 |^q  \sum_{l=1}^\infty (b^n l)^{-(1-\alpha)q} =  \sum_{k=1}^{b^n} | e^{i 2 \pi k b^{-n}} - 1 |^q    b^{-n(1-\alpha)q} \sum_{l=1}^\infty l^{-(1-\alpha)q}.
\end{align*}
Hence, 
\begin{align*}
\limsup_{n\to\infty} b^{n [ -1+ (1-\alpha)q]}  \Sigma_n'' \le     \int_0^1 | e^{i 2 \pi t} - 1 |^q    dt \cdot  \sum_{l=1}^\infty l^{-(1-\alpha)q} =: c_2(\alpha, q)<\infty. 
\end{align*}
It follows that there exist two constants $c_1'(\alpha,q), c_2'(\alpha,q)>0$ such that   
\[
 b^{n [ 1 -(1-\alpha)q]}   c_1'(\alpha, q)\le \Sigma_n \le  b^{n [ 1 -(1-\alpha)q]}   c_2'(\alpha, q) \quad \text{for all $n\ge 1$}.
\]
Hence by the definition \eqref{def-rsigma}, we obtain  the desired equality.

\[
\psi_\xi'(t) = -\frac{\mathbb{E}[\xi e^{-t\xi}]}{\mathbb{E}[e^{-t\xi}]}. 
\] 
Thus, by using the \eqref{xi-cond}, we have 
\begin{align*}
0= \mathbb{E}[\xi' e^{-\xi'}]  =  \mathbb{E}[(x\xi + y) e^{-x \xi -y}]  = - x \psi_\xi'(x)   \mathbb{E}[e^{-x\xi}] e^{-y} + \frac{y}{b}
 =&  - x \frac{\psi_\xi'(x)}{b} + \frac{y}{b} . 
\end{align*}
Hence $y = - x \psi_\xi'(x)$. By
$
1 = \mathbb{E}[be^{-x\xi -y}]  = \exp(\psi_\xi(x) -y), 
$
we have  $y= \psi_\xi(x)$. Therefore $\psi_\xi(x)/x= \psi_\xi'(x)$.

We shall use the same strategy as the proof of  \cite[Theorem 3.4.10]{Rick-Durrett}. Here we give the proof of the case of almost sure convergence in $(7)$ and $(8)$. The case of   convergence in probability is proved similarly. 

We only need to prove that the  conditioned distribution of $Z_n:=\sum_{k=1}^{t_n} X_{n,k}Y_{n,k}$ given $\mathcal{F}_n$ converges to the conditioned distribution of $\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{C}}(0, M_\infty)$ given $\mathcal{F}_\infty$ almost surely. In other words, let $Z_n=\xi_n+i \zeta_n$, we only need to show for any $x,y, t\in\mathbb{R}$: 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-desired}
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\big[\exp\{it(x\xi_n+y\zeta_n)\}\big| \mathcal{F}_n\big]=\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\frac{M_\infty}{2}t^2(x^2+y^2)\Big) \quad a.s.
\end{align}

Now 
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}\big[\exp\{it(x\xi_n+y\zeta_n)\}\big| \mathcal{F}_n\big]=&\mathbb{E}\Big[\exp\Big\{it\sum_{k=1}^{t_n}X_{n,k}\big(x\mathrm{Re}(Y_{n,k})+y\mathrm{Im}(Y_{n,k})\big)\Big\}\big| \mathcal{F}_n\Big]\\
=&\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E} \Big[\exp \Big\{itX_{n,k}(x\mathrm{Re}(Y_{n,k})+y\mathrm{Im}(Y_{n,k})) \Big\} \big| \mathcal{F}_n\Big]\\
=&\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E}[\exp( itA_{n,k}) | \mathcal{F}_n],
\end{align*}
where  $A_{n,k}: =X_{n,k} (x\mathrm{Re}(Y_{n,k})+y\mathrm{Im}(Y_{n,k}) )$ for $1\leq k\leq t_n$. 












{\flushleft \bf Claim B: } One has 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-last-f}
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty }\Big|\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E}[\exp(itA_{n,k})|\mathcal{F}_n]-\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\Big(1-\frac{c t^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\Big)\Big|=0 \quad a.s.
\end{align}
 
 By \cite[Exercise 3.1.1]{Rick-Durrett},
we have 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-last-e}
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\Big(1-\frac{c t^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2(x^2+y^2)\Big)=e^{-\frac{M_\infty}{4}t^2(x^2+y^2)}\,\,a.s.\,\,\text{
where 
$
M_\infty=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{t_n} X_{n,k}^2.
$
}
\end{align}
Then \eqref{eqn-last-f} and \eqref{eqn-last-e} imply that 
\[
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty }\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E}[\exp(itA_{n,k})|\mathcal{F}_n]=e^{-\frac{M_\infty}{4}t^2(x^2+y^2)}\quad a.s.
\]
This is the desired equality \eqref{eqn-desired}.

Now we prove \textbf{Claim B}. By \cite[Lemma 3.3.19]{Rick-Durrett}, one has
\begin{align*}
&\Big|\mathbb{E}[\exp(itA_{n,k})|  \mathcal{F}_n]-1+\frac{ct^2}{4}(x^2+y^2)X_{n,k}^2\Big|
\\
\leq& \mathbb{E}\Big[ \min\left(|tA_{n,k}|^{3},2|tA_{n,k}|^2\right) \big|\mathcal{F}_n\Big]\\
\leq &\mathbb{E}\Big[ |tA_{n,k}|^{3}\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|\leq\varepsilon)\big|\mathcal{F}_n\Big]+\mathbb{E}\Big[ 2|tA_{n,k}|^{2}\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|>\varepsilon)\big|\mathcal{F}_n\Big]\\
\leq&\varepsilon t^3\mathbb{E}\Big[ |A_{n,k}|^{2}\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|\leq\varepsilon)\big|\mathcal{F}_n\Big]+2t^2\mathbb{E}\Big[ |A_{n,k}|^{2}\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|>\varepsilon)\big|\mathcal{F}_n\Big].
\end{align*}
Hence it follows that 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-jkjkh}
&\sum_{k=1}^{t_n}\big|\mathbb{E} [\exp(itA_{n,k})|\mathcal{F}_n]-1+\frac{ct^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\big|\\\nonumber
\leq &\varepsilon t^3\sum_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E}\Big[ |A_{n,k}|^{2}\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|\leq\varepsilon)\mid\mathcal{F}_n\Big]+2t^2\sum_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E}\Big[ |A_{n,k}|^{2}\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|>\varepsilon)\big|\mathcal{F}_n\Big].
\end{align}
Now for any fixed $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$ with $x^2+y^2>0$, one has
\begin{align}\label{eqn-AN-23}
A_{n,k}^2
\leq X_{n,k}^2((\mathrm{Re}(Y_{n,k}))^2+(\mathrm{Im}(Y_{n,k}))^2)(x^2+y^2)
=X_{n,k}^2|Y_{n,k}|^2(x^2+y^2).
\end{align}
This implies that 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-A_n-F_n}
\mathbb{E}[A_{n,k}^2 | \mathcal{F}_n]\leq X_{n,k}^2(x^2+y^2)\mathbb{E}[|Y|^2]=c(x^2+y^2)\cdot X_{n,k}^2.
\end{align}

\begin{align*}
\mathbb{E}[ |A_{n,k}|^{2}\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|>\varepsilon)|\mathcal{F}_n]
\leq (x^2+y^2)\mathbb{E}\Big[|X_{n,k} Y_{n,k}|^2\mathds{1}\Big(|X_{n,k}Y_{n,k}|>\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\Big) \Big| \mathcal{F}_n\Big].
\end{align*}
Hence \eqref{eqn-hjhi} implies that 
\[
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{t_n} \mathbb{E}\left[A_{n,k}^2\mathds{1}(|A_{n,k}|>\varepsilon) | \mathcal{F}_n\right]=0.
\]
Combing with \eqref{eqn-A_n-F_n} and \eqref{eqn-jkjkh}, we have
\begin{align*}
&\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{t_n}\big|\mathbb{E}[\exp(itA_{n,k}) | \mathcal{F}_n]-1+\frac{ct^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\big|\\
\leq &\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\varepsilon t^3 c(x^2+y^2)\sum_{k=1}^{t_n} X_{n,k}^2

\end{align*}
Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, we have 
\begin{align}\label{eqn-important}
\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{t_n}\big|\mathbb{E}[\exp(itA_{n,k}) | \mathcal{F}_n]-1+\frac{ct^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\big|=0 \quad a.s.
\end{align}
Notice that by \eqref{eqn-AN-23}, one has
\[
\mathbb{E}[A_{n,k}^2 |\mathcal{F}_n]=\frac{c}{2}(x^2+y^2)X_{n,k}^2.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{c}{2}(x^2+y^2)X_{n,k}^2=\mathbb{E}[A_{n,k}^2| \mathcal{F}_n]\leq \varepsilon^2+\mathbb{E}\left[A_{n,k}^2\mathds{1}(A_{n,k}>\varepsilon)| \mathcal{F}_n\right]
\]
which implies that 
\[
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{c}{2}(x^2+y^2)X_{n,k}^2\leq \varepsilon^2+\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[A_{n,k}^2\mathds{1}(A_{n,k}>\varepsilon) | \mathcal{F}_n\right]=\varepsilon.
\]
Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary,   for all $1\leq k\leq t_n$, we have
\begin{align}\label{eqn-jijiji}
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{c}{2}(x^2+y^2)X_{n,k}^2=0 \quad  a.s.
\end{align}
Hence almost surely, for $n$ large enough,
\[
\Big|1-\frac{ct^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\Big|\leq 1. 
\] 
By    \cite[Lemma 3.4.3]{Rick-Durrett}, almost surely, for $n$ large enough, we have 
\begin{align*}
& \Big|\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E}[\exp(itA_{n,k})|\mathcal{F}_n]-\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\Big(1-\frac{ct^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\Big)\Big|
\\
\leq & \sum_{k=1}^{t_n}\Big|\mathbb{E}[\exp(itA_{n,k}) | \mathcal{F}_n]-1+\frac{ct^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\Big|.
\end{align*}
Combing with  \eqref{eqn-important}, we have
\[
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty }\Big|\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\mathbb{E}[\exp( itA_{n,k}) |\mathcal{F}_n]-\prod_{k=1}^{t_n}\Big(1-\frac{ct^2}{4} X_{n,k}^2 (x^2+y^2)\Big)\Big|=0 \quad a.s. 
\]
This is the desired equality \eqref{eqn-last-e}.
